title: Diversity in the Living World
intro: Plants and animals around us come in an amazing variety. This chapter teaches you how to observe their differences carefully and how scientists group them so the living world is easier to understand and protect.

branches.label: Observing Variety
details: Different plants and animals around us
Bird calls, leaf shapes, ways of moving

branches.label: Biodiversity
details: Variety of life in a region
Plants and animals depend on each other

sections.heading: Variety in Plants and Animals Around Us
bullets: Even within one park, you can spot grasses, bushes, and tall trees alongside birds, butterflies, ants, and monkeys.
Each kind of bird has its own unique chirp; this is one example of diversity in nature.
Plants differ in stem hardness, height, leaf shape and arrangement, and flower colour and scent.
Animals differ in where they live, what they eat, and how they move.
Observing without disturbing — not plucking leaves or chasing animals — is part of respecting living things.

sections.heading: Why We Group Plants and Animals
bullets: Grouping is sorting things by common features, like arranging books by subject.
It makes the huge variety of life easier to understand and study.
The same set of plants can be grouped differently — by height, by flowers present, or by leaf shape.
Different scientists may pick different features, so groupings can vary.
Grouping helps in identifying, naming, and conserving plants and animals.

sections.heading: Grouping Plants by Stem and Leaves
bullets: Herbs are short plants with soft, green stems (e.g., tulsi, mint).
Shrubs are medium-sized plants with hard, branching stems near the base (e.g., rose, lemon).
Trees are tall plants with thick, hard, woody stems and branches high up (e.g., neem, mango).
Leaves can have parallel venation (veins running side-by-side, like in grass and maize) or reticulate venation (veins forming a net, like in mango and hibiscus).
Leaf shape, edge, and arrangement (alternate, opposite, whorled) all help in identification.

sections.heading: Grouping Plants by Roots and Seeds
bullets: Taproot system: one main root with smaller roots branching off (mango, gram, mustard).
Fibrous root system: many thin roots of similar size from the base of the stem (grass, wheat, maize).
Plants with parallel-veined leaves usually have fibrous roots.
Plants with reticulate-veined leaves usually have taproots.
Seeds with two halves (cotyledons) are dicots; seeds with one cotyledon are monocots — gram is a dicot, maize is a monocot.

sections.heading: Grouping Animals
bullets: By habitat: land animals (cow, dog), water animals (fish), animals that live in both land and water (frog), and animals of the air (birds, bats).
By food: herbivores eat plants (cow, deer), carnivores eat other animals (lion, tiger), and omnivores eat both (humans, crow).
By movement: walking, crawling, flying, swimming, hopping — each suited to where the animal lives.
By body parts: number of legs, presence of wings, scales, feathers, or fur.
Two animals can share some features (both can fly) yet differ in others (a bird has feathers, a bat has fur).

sections.heading: Biodiversity and Why It Matters
bullets: Biodiversity is the variety of plants, animals, and other living things found in a particular region.
Members of a biodiversity depend on each other — trees give shelter to birds, animals spread seeds.
Protecting one species often helps protect many others connected to it.
Human actions like cutting forests or polluting water reduce biodiversity.
Simple steps like planting trees and not littering help preserve the living world around us.

key_takeaways: The living world has huge variety; we group plants and animals by common features to make sense of it.
Plants are grouped as herbs, shrubs, and trees by height and stem hardness.
Leaves can have parallel or reticulate venation, and roots can be taproot or fibrous — these features go together.
Seeds with two cotyledons are dicots; seeds with one cotyledon are monocots.
Animals can be grouped by habitat, food, body parts, or how they move.
Biodiversity matters because every living thing has a role and they all depend on one another.

glossary.definition: The variety of plants, animals, and other living things in a particular area.
A short plant with a soft, green stem.
A medium-sized plant with a hard, branching stem near the base.
A tall plant with a thick, hard, woody stem and branches high up.
A root system with one main thick root and smaller side roots.
A root system with many thin roots of similar size growing from the stem base.
Leaf veins that run side by side, like in grass and maize.
Leaf veins that form a net pattern, like in mango and hibiscus.
A plant whose seed has two cotyledons (seed leaves), e.g., gram, mango.
A plant whose seed has only one cotyledon, e.g., maize, wheat.
An animal that eats only plants, e.g., cow, deer.
An animal that eats other animals, e.g., lion, tiger.
An animal that eats both plants and animals, e.g., crow, humans.
